title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Two things happen on this page (Opusc. Anal. I, pp. 208-209).

(1) Scholion §56, item III. Euler starts from the partial-fraction identity of §36:
π cos nπ sin ωπ / (ω sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π) = 1/(n²−ω²) − 1/((1−n)²−ω²) − 1/((1+n)²−ω²) + 1/((2−n)²−ω²) + 1/((2+n)²−ω²) − …
In modern form this is Σ_{k∈Z} (−1)^k/((n+k)²−ω²). It follows from (1/2ω)[π/sin(n−ω)π − π/sin(n+ω)π].
- At n = 1/2 both sides vanish: cos nπ = 0, and the terms cancel in pairs.
- So Euler differentiates with respect to n. The left side becomes −π² sin nπ sin ωπ (1 + cos(n−ω)π cos(n+ω)π) / (ω (sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π)²). This is correct, since 1 + cos(n−ω)π cos(n+ω)π = cos²nπ + cos²ωπ. Each term 1/(x²−ω²) of the right side differentiates to ∓2x/(x²−ω²)².
- Setting n = 1/2 and dividing by −32 gives
π² sin ωπ / (32 ω cos²ωπ) = Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k (2k+1)/((2k+1)²−4ω²)².
- Letting ω→0 gives π³/32 = 1 − 1/3³ + 1/5³ − …, i.e. β(3) = π³/32, which Euler notes is 'aliunde constat'.
Euler then remarks that the series of the present problem (the interpolation series of §55, Corollary 1) is 'much harder' and deserves further study, which he undertakes in Problem 6.

(2) Problem 6 (§57). The series is
s = 1/n + n/(1(1−n)) + n(1−n)/(1·2(1+n)) + n(1−n)(1+n)/(1·2·3(2−n)) + …,
already known to equal π/sin nπ. Since the law of the terms is 'interrupted', Euler splits s = P + Q into even and odd parts. He uses the angle-expansions
- cos μΦ/cos Φ = Σ [(1−μ²)(9−μ²)…/(2k)!] sin^{2k}Φ, i.e. a ₂F₁((1+μ)/2,(1−μ)/2;1/2;sin²Φ);
- sin νΦ/cos Φ = Σ [ν(4−ν²)(16−ν²)…/(2k+1)!] sin^{2k+1}Φ.
For P he matches the ratios of factors, which forces μ = 1−2n, because (1−μ)(1+μ) = 4n(1−n), (3−μ)(3+μ) = 4(1+n)(2−n), and so on. He then:
- multiplies by sin^{2n−1}Φ cos Φ dΦ and integrates from 0;
- sets sin Φ = 1/2 (Φ = 30°), which makes the powers 2^{2k} cancel;
- obtains P = 2^{2n+1} ∫_0^{π/6} sin^{2n−1}Φ cos(1−2n)Φ dΦ.
For Q he takes ν = 2n, multiplies by sin^{−2n}Φ cos Φ dΦ and integrates. This is completed on the next page, giving Q = 2^{2−2n} ∫_0^{π/6} sin^{−2n}Φ sin 2nΦ dΦ.
The result (p. 210) is
π/sin nπ = 4∫_0^{π/6} cos(1−2n)Φ (2 sin Φ)^{2n−1} dΦ + 4∫_0^{π/6} sin 2nΦ (2 sin Φ)^{−2n} dΦ, for 0<n<1.
Corollaries 58-59 recast this with 2n = (1∓λ)/2. Euler remarks that he has checked it in all evaluable cases but gives no direct proof.

Modern reading of (2): with z = e^{2iΦ}, the two integrals are the real parts of a Beta integral B(n,1−n) = ∫ t^{n−1}(1−t)^{−n} dt. That integral is taken along a path from 0 to 1 through the sixth root of unity e^{iπ/3}, the point where |t| = |1−t| = 1. The paths are unit-circle arcs centred at 0 and at 1. The choice sin Φ = 1/2 is exactly what puts the endpoint there. Euler instead derives the identity by series manipulation and is content with case verification.
errors: The §56 identity as transcribed on the previous page has sin nπ in the numerator. It must be cos nπ (π cos nπ sin ωπ/(ω sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π)); otherwise item I (π² cos nπ/sin²nπ) and the remark 'ob cos nπ = 0 etiam ipsa series evanescit' make no sense. This is likely a transcription or print slip, not a mathematical error.
In the series π² sin ωπ/(32ω cos²ωπ) = 1/(1−4ω²)² − 3/(9−4ω²)² + 5/(25−4ω²)² − 7/(49−4ω²)² …, the trailing sign should be '+ etc.' (the signs alternate), not '− etc.'.
Problem 6's integral representation requires 0<n<1 for convergence at Φ=0 (lower limit tacitly 0). Euler states it 'si n sit numerus quicunque' without restriction.
The final identity (p. 210) is asserted only on the basis that it is already known from elsewhere and checked case by case. No independent proof is given; the derivation is correct, however.

ideas.what: Differentiating the alternating partial-fraction expansion in the shift parameter n and evaluating at n=1/2 where it degenerates, giving the generating function Σ(−1)^k(2k+1)/((2k+1)²−4ω²)² = π² sin ωπ/(32ω cos²ωπ)
ideas.modern_name: Mittag-Leffler / partial fractions of trigonometric functions; derivative giving a generating function for odd Dirichlet beta values
ideas.where_published: Introductio in analysin infinitorum I, ch. X; E41/E61 for β(3)=π³/32

ideas.what: Expansions of cos μΦ/cos Φ and sin νΦ/cos Φ in powers of sin Φ
ideas.modern_name: Hypergeometric (₂F₁) expansions of cos(μ arcsin x)/√(1−x²), sin(ν arcsin x)/√(1−x²)
ideas.where_published: Institutiones calculi differentialis and various papers on angle multiplication

ideas.what: Even/odd splitting of an interpolation series for π/sin nπ and evaluation of each part as an incomplete trigonometric integral over [0,π/6] (sin Φ = 1/2)
ideas.modern_name: Representation of B(n,1−n) along a path through e^{iπ/3}; incomplete Beta / generalized log-sine-type integrals at π/3
ideas.usually_credited_to: unsure (the specific identity seems not to be standardly cited)

missed.claim: The final identity π/sin nπ = 4∫_0^{π/6} cos(1−2n)Φ(2 sin Φ)^{2n−1}dΦ + 4∫_0^{π/6} sin 2nΦ(2 sin Φ)^{−2n}dΦ, which Euler verified only case by case, is precisely the Beta integral B(n,1−n) deformed to the two-arc path 0 → e^{iπ/3} → 1 (arcs of |t−1|=1 and |t|=1). The 30° choice is the sixth root of unity where |t|=|1−t|=1. Euler's series route thus anticipates contour deformation, and is related to the π/3 evaluations in the modern theory of generalized log-sine integrals (Borwein–Straub).
missed.quote: Nunc post integrationem statuatur sin.Φ = 1/2, seu Φ = 30°
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This gives a historical precursor for log-sine / Mahler-measure-type integrals at π/3, and a proof that Euler lacked. It is of modest interest only; the identity itself is elementary from a modern standpoint.

deep.surprise_reason: Item III is a routine rederivation of β(3)=π³/32 via a correct but standard differentiation trick. Problem 6's split into integrals over [0,π/6] is a curious, little-cited identity that Euler only checked case by case. It has an elegant modern explanation as a deformed Beta-integral path through e^{iπ/3}, but nothing here would genuinely surprise a specialist.
transcription_corrections: '111. Si capiatur' should read 'III. Si capiatur' (item III of the Scholion).
'Quin adeo casus in corollario 1 euolutus, eft maxime eft particularis' should read '… euolutus, et maxime est particularis'.
In the series 1/(1−4ωω)² − 3/(9−4ωω)² + 5/(25−4ωω)² − 7/(49−4ωω)² …, the trailing sign is mathematically '+ etc.'.
On the previous page, the §56 left-hand side should contain cos.nπ (not sin.nπ) in the numerator.
On the next page, the uncertain '[?]' factor in Q is confirmed as 2^{2−2n}.
